name: Mixed Debate
description: Two opposing worldviews merged into one map. Beliefs 0-4 belong to a collectivist environmentalist; beliefs 5-9 belong to an individualist capitalist. Within each group beliefs are compatible; across groups they clash. This produces two visible clusters in the network graph.
beliefs: The common good should take precedence over individual profit
Nature has intrinsic value beyond its utility to humans
Wealth inequality is the root cause of most social problems
Corporations must be strictly regulated to protect people
Cooperation, not competition, drives the best outcomes
Individual achievement is the engine of human progress
Free markets naturally produce the most prosperous societies
Wealth creation benefits everyone through economic growth
Excessive regulation stifles innovation and personal freedom
Competition is the natural and healthy state of human affairs

justifications.0-5: Collectivist prioritization of the common good directly opposes individualist emphasis on personal achievement as the driver of progress.
justifications.0-6: The belief that common good outweighs individual profit is fundamentally at odds with faith in unregulated free markets.
justifications.0-4: Both beliefs affirm that cooperative, group-oriented approaches produce the best outcomes for society.
justifications.2-7: The claim that wealth inequality causes social problems directly contradicts the belief that wealth creation benefits everyone.
justifications.3-8: Strict corporate regulation clashes with the view that regulation stifles innovation and freedom.
justifications.4-9: The belief that cooperation drives the best outcomes is contradicted by the claim that competition is the natural and healthy human state.
justifications.1-6: Intrinsic value of nature conflicts with a market-driven worldview that values nature primarily as a resource.
justifications.5-6: Individual achievement and free markets are mutually reinforcing pillars of the same individualist worldview.
justifications.0-1: Prioritizing the common good aligns with valuing nature beyond its utility — both subordinate profit to broader values.
justifications.7-8: Wealth creation through growth and opposition to excessive regulation reflect the same pro-market economic philosophy.
